title: Six Indian American Students Named 2026 Davidson Fellows, Win Up to $100,000
excerpt: Aditya Sengupta of Bellevue, Washington, won the $100,000 Laureate award for a machine-learning system that predicts clear-air turbulence; five others earned $50,000 and $25,000 scholarships for work on nuclear safety, malaria, drug discovery and more.
body:
• Six Indian American students are among the 2026 Davidson Fellows, earning scholarships of up to $100,000 for ambitious scientific work on aviation safety, crop disease, nuclear energy, malaria prevention and drug discovery.
  • Aditya Sengupta, 18, of Bellevue, Washington, won the top honor — the $100,000 Davidson Fellow Laureate scholarship — for ForeCAT, a machine-learning system that predicts clear-air turbulence.
  • Tanishka Aglave, Hitaishi Chillara, Praadhyumn Indaana and Rajarshi Mandal each earned $50,000 scholarships, while Pavan Subramani was awarded $25,000.
  • The Davidson Fellows Scholarship is among the most prestigious honors for students 18 and younger, recognizing significant work across science, technology, mathematics, literature, music and philosophy.

Six Indian American students have been named 2026 Davidson Fellows, joining one of the most selective cohorts of young scholars in the United States. The Davidson Institute announced the recipients this week, awarding scholarships worth up to $100,000 to students 18 and younger for significant work ranging from predicting dangerous turbulence for aircraft to accelerating drug discovery.

Six names, five states

The headline honor went to Aditya Sengupta, 18, of Bellevue, Washington, who received the $100,000 Davidson Fellow Laureate scholarship — the program's top award. Four students earned $50,000 scholarships: Tanishka Aglave of Valrico, Florida; Hitaishi Chillara of Leander, Texas; Praadhyumn Indaana of Montvale, New Jersey; and Rajarshi Mandal of Lexington, Massachusetts. Pavan Subramani, 17, of Morgantown, West Virginia, received a $25,000 scholarship.

The Davidson Institute awards its $100,000, $50,000 and $25,000 scholarships each year to students 18 and younger for extraordinary work in fields spanning science, technology and mathematics to literature, music and philosophy. It is widely regarded as one of the nation's most prestigious honors for young people.

From turbulence to drug discovery

Sengupta's inspiration came from something familiar to millions of air travelers: unexpectedly rough skies. After experiencing sudden and frightening turbulence on flights, he began asking why clear-air turbulence — which strikes without visible clouds or storms — remains so difficult to predict. His answer was ForeCAT, a machine-learning system that combines atmospheric physics with computing to predict the likelihood and severity of the phenomenon. Sengupta says his results showed significant improvements over the forecasting approaches currently used in aviation.

"Being named a Davidson Fellow is an incredible honor because it gives me the opportunity to join a community of young people who are curious, ambitious, and passionate about using their ideas to improve lives."

— Aditya Sengupta, 2026 Davidson Fellow Laureate

The other Indian American winners tackled problems with equally concrete stakes. Indaana spent eight months building a physics-guided neural network trained on more than 10,000 real experiments to predict critical heat flux — the threshold at which a nuclear reactor's cooling process can begin to fail. His model cut the average prediction error from about 63% with conventional formulas to 5.5%, work the Times of India spotlighted this week for its potential to make carbon-free electricity safer and more efficient.

Mandal built a simulation of how malaria actually spreads under realistic conditions and used it to evaluate where mosquito nets deliver the largest effect. "With the same number of nets, my approach prevented twice as many infections," he said of his work. Chillara developed a computational framework combining universe simulations, telescope observations and machine learning to test whether the colors and brightnesses measured by sky surveys contain clues about a black hole's mass. Subramani's project, "The Hybridization of Generative Diffusion Models with Molecular Dynamics Simulations," offers a novel method to accelerate drug discovery.

A pipeline of recognition

Several of the winners arrived at the Davidson stage with honors already behind them. Aglave previously earned the H. Robert Horvitz Prize for Fundamental Research at the Regeneron International Science and Engineering Fair for her investigation of a natural alternative treatment for citrus greening, a disease that threatens citrus farming worldwide — she injected infected trees' trunks with an extract from the curry leaf tree and showed the method could sustainably manage the disease. The progression from science-fair prizes to a Davidson Fellowship is a familiar one: the program's alumni include some of the most decorated young researchers in the country.

What comes next

The scholarships give each student significant freedom to carry their work forward — into undergraduate research, startup labs, or graduate study. For the Indian American community, which watched its young scientists collect a growing share of the nation's top youth honors this year, the six Fellows are the latest evidence of a deepening pipeline of talent. The Davidson Institute's full list of 2026 Fellows spans disciplines from science to music; for these six, the recognition is both a reward and an invitation to keep building.
